Thereby
thâr-bī'
adv. (compound relative; rendering Hebrew bo of means, Greek di' autou)
A compound of there and by, meaning by that, by means of it, or sometimes near it. English still keeps it in formal prose, where it marks the instrument or the consequence of what has just been said.

Biblical Definition

Thereby means by that means, and Scripture uses it to fasten a consequence to its cause. Ezekiel states the principle of personal responsibility in its sharpest form: “When the righteous turneth from his righteousness, and committeth iniquity, he shall even die thereby” (Ezekiel 33:18) — the death is not arbitrary but is the fruit of the iniquity itself. Ecclesiastes applies the same logic to ordinary labour: “he that cleaveth wood shall be endangered thereby” (Ecclesiastes 10:9), a plain observation that work carries its own risks and wisdom consists partly in knowing them. The word also serves for mere proximity, and there it becomes the language of desolation: Jeremiah says of a doomed city that “every one that passeth thereby shall be astonished and hiss because of all the plagues thereof” (Jeremiah 19:8), and again that no son of man does “pass thereby” at all (Jeremiah 51:43). A place so wasted that travellers no longer take the road past it is the prophet's picture of judgment complete.

Webster 1828 Definition

A compound adverb meaning by that, by means of it, or near it. In Scripture it ties a consequence to its cause — the man who turns from righteousness shall die thereby — and describes the desolation at which every passer-by is astonished.

expand to see more

THEREBY, adv. [there and by.] By that; by means of that; in consequence of that.

2. Near that place; as, he passed thereby.

3. It refers to a cause, an instrument, or a means before mentioned.

4. It is retained in the legal, formal and scriptural style.

5. In Scripture, he shall even die thereby, Ezek. 33; every one that passeth thereby shall be astonished, Jer. 19.

Key Scripture

Ezekiel 33:18 — "When the righteous turneth from his righteousness, and committeth iniquity, he shall even die thereby."

Ecclesiastes 10:9 — "Whoso removeth stones shall be hurt therewith; and he that cleaveth wood shall be endangered thereby."

Jeremiah 19:8 — "And I will make this city desolate, and an hissing; every one that passeth thereby shall be astonished and hiss because of all the plagues thereof."

Jeremiah 51:43 — "Her cities are a desolation, a dry land, and a wilderness, a land wherein no man dwelleth, neither doth any son of man pass thereby."

Modern Corruption

The doctrine of Ezekiel 33 is regularly conscripted for two opposite errors: a works-righteousness that makes standing before God depend on the last thing a man did, and a false assurance that treats a past profession as proof against any present course.

expand to see more

Ezekiel is addressing the covenant nation and the question of who shall live in the land, and his answer refuses both a hereditary presumption and a merely formal righteousness. But the passage does not overturn justification by faith alone, and it must not be read as though salvation were held on a running tally. The Reformed doctrine of perseverance answers precisely here: those whom God has effectually called and sanctified can neither totally nor finally fall away, but shall certainly persevere to the end. A man who turns from his righteousness and dies thereby demonstrates what his righteousness was, rather than losing a salvation he possessed.

The opposite abuse is more common in evangelical churches and does more harm. A profession made once is treated as a receipt, so that no present course of life can call it into question, and the warnings of Scripture are explained away as hypothetical. But the same confession that denies final apostasy insists that perseverance is the genuine fruit of regeneration and not a bare formula — not once saved, always saved as a slogan detached from a changed life. Ezekiel 33 is preached rightly when it drives the presumptuous to examine themselves and the fearful to Christ.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew expresses means by the preposition be with a suffix, the same form that gives therein; context distinguishes place from instrument. Greek uses dia with the genitive for means and para for proximity.

expand to see more

Hebrew be of instrument — the preposition in used for the means by which a thing is done.

Hebrew 'avon (H5771) — iniquity, guilt, the punishment of iniquity; the thing by which the turner dies.

Hebrew baqa' (H1234) — to cleave or split; the woodcutter's work in Ecclesiastes 10:9.

Greek dia (G1223) — through, by means of; with the genitive, the standard preposition of instrument.

Saxon þærbi — the Old English compound of there and by.

Usage

"Of a consequence bound to its cause: When the righteous turneth from his righteousness... he shall even die thereby (Ezekiel 33:18)."

"Of the ordinary risks attending labour: he that cleaveth wood shall be endangered thereby (Ecclesiastes 10:9)."

"Of a desolation that travellers stop to marvel at: every one that passeth thereby shall be astonished (Jeremiah 19:8)."
